en: In the language of India: *Karmāntavibhaṅga-nāma*. In the language of Tibet: *Las kyi mtha’ rnam par ’byed pa zhes bya ba* (The Detailed Analysis of the Limits of Action). Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva!

Having prostrated to the fourfold emptiness that is free from beginning, middle, and end, one should apply the definitive arrangement according to the distinctions of the stages of total purity and complete purification. Arising from the three types of primordial wisdom, the four elements, the six faculties, the five aggregates, the nine apertures, and for the most part the three realms of existence, consist of the four modes of birth: birth from an egg, birth from a womb, [birth from moisture, and miraculous birth].

The third is born from warmth and moisture; the fourth is also miraculous birth. As taught by the beginningless Buddha, through the cultivation of the three consciousnesses, the karma practiced throughout the three times has the three consciousnesses as its cause. What is called the "three wisdoms" is also mere appearance; first, ignorance is to be known, and second, that which arises from the mind is likewise.

Third, these so-called "minds" are described as the three emptinesses. From the three emptinesses, the winds arise; they abide in that very [reality] and everywhere. They become its very vehicle, for even the self is empty. From consciousness, the wind arises; from that, fire truly arises; from that, water arises; and from that, earth arises. (146a)

From those, the aggregates arise; from those, the sense bases arise. From those, the natures of primordial wisdom—numbering one hundred and sixty—arise again: in some instances, momentary freedom from passion and fear; in some, the very state of peace; in some, love, compassion, discernment, and mental engagement; in some, craving, conceptualization, the knowable, knowledge, and a sense of shame.

The elements and non-virtues lack intrinsic nature; grasping and so forth, in some cases hunger and thirst, in some cases stinginess, in some cases fear and feeling—these natures of the mind have the wisdom of appearance as their cause. Momentary passion, likewise joy, in some cases malice and power, in some cases pride and likewise exertion, in some cases delight and forcefulness, in some cases [the absence of] anything at all.

In some cases there is steadfastness and power; in some, speech becomes clear. In some there is truth and untruth; in some, there is an instigator who incites. In some there is heroism and diligence; in some, shamelessness and provocation. In some there is fierce wonder; in some, hostility, the very nature of a giver, wickedness, crookedness, and even graceful charm—all these arise from the mind.

Forgetfulness, occasional delusion, distraction, laziness, fatigue, and occasionally remaining silent—these should be known as doubt; they arise at the time of ignorance. These natures of primordial wisdom are explained as being fifty-four.
When the four [elements] have become distinct, so too do the aggregates and the sense faculties.
Through the distinction between night and day, they enter again and again; having passed away from each of the four [continents], it is likewise with the aggregates and the sense faculties.
By this sequence, they dissolve just as they previously came:
first the earth goes to water, and water goes to fire.
Just as it came before, it dissolves through this sequence: first, earth enters water; water dissolves into fire;
fire follows after wind; wind enters into consciousness.
Consciousness, having reached the state of *dhāraṇā*, then enters the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).
I shall dissolve into the wind; the wind enters into consciousness. Having proceeded to the grasping of consciousness, one then enters into the clear light.
Therefore, having become a *gandharva*, one is born impelled by karma.
(Tanaka: *karmacoditam*)
Thus, having been born again and again in the oceans of existence, time and again.
After that, having become a gandharva, one is born impelled by karma; thus, throughout thousands of births, being born again and again,
the world does not reach the further shore due to the natural whirlpool of delusion.
The thorough knowledge of appearances is beyond the reach of logicians.

The nature [of things] revolves and is entirely delusive; it is not the domain of logicians. As long as beings have not attained the thorough knowledge of appearances, even the convergence of appearances is extremely difficult to find.
Others conceptualize it thus: "It consists of *rajas*, *tamas*, and *sattva*."
Even those who have attained the appearances will find it extremely difficult to attain them again. Know that these are dust, darkness, and essence; this is how they are conceptualized by others.
These three appearances [arise] from the abandonment of the knowledge of intrinsic nature.
(In the original, *svābhāva* is corrected to *svabhāva*).
And these three types of knowledge are considered the causes of both cyclic existence and nirvana.
In order to abandon the knowledge of the nature of these very three appearances, these three wisdoms are asserted as the causes of both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa.
Where the natures of the appearances abide, that is the locus of merit and demerit.
What is the nature [of the appearances]?
Therefore,
for one who is purified by the three appearances, the state of the Sugata is certain.
Where does the nature of appearance abide? There, the purification of the three appearances—sin and merit—is the definitive abode of the Sugata.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others such as Kapila [abide there].
Those who are utterly deluded by the appearance of primordial nature (prakṛti) are likewise so in every respect regarding purification.

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others such as Kapila, are utterly deluded regarding the appearance of intrinsic nature; they are likewise [deluded] in every respect concerning that which is completely pure.

Even throughout infinite eons, by giving one’s head, jewels, and so forth, if appearances are not purified, the fruit of enlightenment will not be attained. Even throughout infinite eons, likewise through ethical discipline, patience, and so forth, if appearances are not purified, the fruit of enlightenment will not be attained. Even throughout infinite eons, through the meditative absorption of the mantra body...

If appearances are not completely purified, the fruit of enlightenment will not be attained. When these three appearances are purified, omniscience is certain. This is attained through the very succession of the lineage of gurus, and not by any other means. Like clouds possessing the form of the sound of thunder, those that arise from the expanse of space circle the ten directions and remain in that very place.

Just as they are seen to vanish once again, so too do the consciousnesses emerge from the state of luminosity and, having perished, abide in various natural forms and vanish right there. This concludes the *Karmāntavibhaṅga*, composed by the venerable Ārya Nāgabodhi.

Having respectfully heard this from the presence of the Indian preceptor and venerable master Maṇikaśrījñāna and the great venerable master Rabaṃti, it was translated, edited, and finalized by the translator Chag Lo-tsā-ba, the Śākya bhikṣu Chos-rje-dpal. 147a.
